text.p: For millions of American families with young kids, McDonald's will be hard to avoid next month.
Fast-food marketer McDonald's Corp. has teamed up with Oak Brook, Ill,.-based Ty Inc., maker of the Beanie Babies toy sensation, for what may be the biggest Happy Meal promotion of the year.
Beginning April 11, McDonald's will hand out one of 10 Ty Teenie Beanie Babies with its Happy Meals.
The Teenie Beanies will be scaled-down versions of the original hand-sized, beanbag-like animal creations, which may be this year's hottest toy for the under-10 set.
For Ty, which does not advertise, license or otherwise publicly promote its product, the McDonald's deal represents a rare foray into conventional toy marketing techniques.
"This is a first for our company. It's something we both (Ty and McDonald's) thought would be advantageous," said Ty Warner, president, designer and owner, in a rare interview.

The McDonald's Happy Meal promotion offered an opportunity to reach a whole group of kids who haven't yet been exposed to his product, Warner said. Ty specifically hopes to reach kids in inner-city Hispanic and African-American neighbourhoods, which have had limited access to Beanies.

Beanie Babies currently are sold in small speciality stores, generally located in upscale neighbourhoods, Warner said. The toys have no distribution in mass merchandise outlets. Though unusual for a toy marketer, the system has worked for Ty, which last year was ranked the No. 8 best-selling toy by Playthings magazine and the No. 1 toy sold in speciality stores.
"This is really the first major blockbuster hit sold through the speciality channel," said Frank Reysen, editor of Playthings.

"We really did it to expand our product to children who wouldn't be shopping in upscale shopping malls. We saw McDonald's as the best avenue to get these kids to see them," said Warner. "If a child brings a Teenie Beanie to school and starts to collect them, so much the better."

McDonald's declined to confirm or deny the Ty co-promotion, but Shelley Rosen, senior vice president of Simon Marketing Inc., the Oak Brook, Ill.-based promotion company that handles McDonald's Happy Meal promotions, said last week the Ty deal was a go.
Ty has no plans to change his marketing methods, which fuel demand by tightly controlling distribution, frequently introducing new Beanie animal designs and retiring older ones.
"The scarcity strategy has worked for them," said Reysen. "They're marketed as a collectible in much the same way that trading cards are sold."
Demand for Beanies, which have been around since 1993, shows no sign of letting up.

"Nothing in the toy industry has ever been at this level of demand," Warner said. Last year, Ty did more than $1.5 billion in business wholesale. Beanies, which generally retail for $4.99, are priced for kids to buy them with their allowance money.

But the collectible craze has caught the attention of adults, who often buy up a store's supply of Beanies and sell them for $20 to $30 over the Internet. Retired Beanies can sell for $100 or more over the Internet.
"Adults have gotten greedy," said Warner. "It's not fair, and it's something we need to work on."
Though toy fads based on limited distribution generally have a short shelf life -- witness the Tyco Tickle Me Elmo craze of just three months ago -- Warner believes Beanies have staying power.
"These are not Smurfs or Trolls, which all looked alike," Warner said. "This is not a fad. It won't be over by the evening news."
